catalog_quote: [p. 4] Accent tonique. Les Wanyaruanda parlent lentement et en chantant («wararandira» = ils scandent, parler lentement), les Warundi au contraire parlent plus vite («wararuga n'ingoga»). Bien placer l'accent tonique est plus important encore en kirundi que dans les autres langues Bantu. Souvent on n'est pas compris faute de cela. La même syllabe d'un mot est souvent différemment accentuée selon qu'elle se trouve au commencement, à la fin ou intercalée. On peut dire toutefois que très souvent l'avant-dernière syllabe porte l'accent long. Ex.: umugurōba, aragīye, umwāna, etc. [p. 79] Cette langue (Kitwa) autant que nous avons pu le savoir est identique au Kirundi quant à tous les éléments grammaticaux. Tout: classes, accord, pronoms, numéraux, conjugaison est le même, tellement qu'il est superflu de donner un sommaire du Kitwa pour ne pas nous répéter.

new_statements.translation: [p. 4] Tonic accent. The Banyarwanda speak slowly and in a sing-song ... the Barundi on the contrary speak faster. Placing the tonic accent correctly is even more important in Kirundi than in the other Bantu languages. Often one is not understood for want of it. The same syllable of a word is often accented differently according to whether it stands at the beginning, at the end, or in between. One may say however that very often the penultimate syllable carries the long accent. Ex.: umugorōba, aragīye, umwāna, etc. [p. 79] This language (Kitwa), as far as we could learn, is identical to Kirundi in all grammatical elements.

(1) QUOTE: p. 4 (PDF p. 515) 'Accent tonique' paragraph is there word for word: 'Les Wanyaruanda parlent lentement et en chantant («wararandira» = ils scandent, parler lentement), les Warundi au contraire parlent plus vite («wararuga n'ingoga»). Bien placer l'accent tonique est plus important encore en kirundi que dans les autres langues Bantu. Souvent on n'est pas compris faute de cela. La même syllabe d'un mot est souvent différemment accentuée selon qu'elle se trouve au commencement, à la fin ou intercalé…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Impressionistic 1902 missionary statement for Kirundi as spoken by all of Urundi (Watwa included), extended to Kitwa only via the author's claim of full grammatical identity: accent placement is meaningful (mis-accenting causes misunderstanding), the accent of a given syllable shifts with its position, and 'very often' the penultimate syllable bears a 'long accent' -- the examples are all words with a lexically long penultimate vowel (umugoróoba, aragíiye, umwáana), so this is a length/prominence tendency, not a fixed-stress rule; modern analyses treat Kirundi as tonal with contrastive vowel length.
new_statements.exceptions: Only that the same syllable is 'differently accented' depending on initial/final/medial position; no rule given. Menard 1908 (Kirundi proper) explicitly treats accent as lexical with minimal pairs and no fixed position.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms; the positional remark ('au commencement, a la fin ou intercalee') hints at phrase-position effects. Statement is about Kirundi generally, not elicited from Kitwa speakers specifically.
new_statements.identity_note: Rundi-Kitwa (rund1241) is a barely-attested, now-extinct lect known only from van der Burgt (1902, 1903): a lexically divergent in-group speech of the Batwa of Urundi (recorded mainly at Uzige/Rusizi valley and on the Ruvubu) which he states is grammatically identical to Kirundi. The only prosodic statement in the defining source is the 'Accent tonique' paragraph of the Kirundi grammar proper (p. 4), i.e. a statement about Kirundi at large (Glottolog rund1242, ISO run), which the author frames as the language 'tous parlent.. meme les Watwa'. Nothing accent-specific is said about Kitwa itself. Any catalog entry should therefore either inherit from Kirundi (rund1242, itself recorded as the named source could not be reached: Meeussen 1959) or be left empty.

sources.note: Kirundi proper, not Kitwa: 'accent' distinguishes minimal pairs (kuraba/kuraba etc.), is realised as vowel length/quality, monosyllabic radicals unaccented, disyllabic radicals either unaccented or accented on first syllable, polysyllables in various patterns -- i.e. lexical, no fixed position; separate 'accent de narration' (emphatic lengthening). Batwa mentioned only as potters (p. ~x).

sources.note: Kitwa supplement (p. 79, PDF p. 590): Kitwa 'est identique au Kirundi quant a tous les elements grammaticaux' -- nothing on accent. Kirundi grammar 'Accent tonique' (p. 4, PDF p. 515): placing the accent correctly is crucial for being understood; the same syllable is accented differently by position; 'tres souvent l'avant-derniere syllabe porte l'accent long' (ex. umugoroba, aragiye, umwana with penult macron). Closing remark pp. 106-108: Kitwa may be merely archaic Kirundi.
